original_value: Since their introduction a year ago, distributional approaches to reinforcement learning (distributional RL) have produced strong results relative to the standard approach which models expected values (expected RL). However, aside from convergence guarantees, there have been few theoretical results investigating the reasons behind the improvements distributional RL provides. In this paper we begin the investigation into this fundamental question by analyzing the differences in the tabular, linear approximation, and non-linear approximation settings. We prove that in many realizations of the tabular and linear approximation settings, distributional RL behaves exactly the same as expected RL. In cases where the two methods behave differently, distributional RL can in fact hurt performance when it does not induce identical behaviour. We then continue with an empirical analysis comparing distributional and expected RL methods in control settings with non-linear approximators to tease apart where the improvements from distributional RL methods are coming from.

result.paraphrase: Since their introduction a year earlier, distributional reinforcement learning methods have delivered strong results compared with the standard expected-value-based approach (expected RL). Yet, apart from convergence guarantees, there have been few theoretical studies examining why distributional RL improves performance. In this paper, we begin addressing that fundamental question by analyzing the tabular, linear approximation, and non-linear approximation settings. We show that in many instances of the tabular and linear approximation settings, distributional RL behaves exactly like expected RL. When the two methods do differ, distributional RL can actually harm performance if it does not produce identical behavior. We then present an empirical comparison of distributional and expected RL in control settings with non-linear approximators to disentangle the sources of distributional RL’s gains.
